quote: Cooperation is unstable, in both game theory and evolutionary biology, without some kind of punishment for defection.
content: Stated as a law, and it is not one. Nowak (2006) reviews five distinct mechanisms that sustain cooperation — kin selection, direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity via reputation, network structure and group selection — none of which requires costly punishment. Where punishment has been tested directly, it often destroys more value than it protects: in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with a punishment option, the players who earned the most were those who never punished (Dreber et al., 2008). Withholding cooperation from defectors, or simply choosing other partners, does the work; the essay's premise is one mechanism among several, promoted to a necessity.

quote: then that is punishment of non-punishers, a far more dangerous idiom that can lock an equilibrium in place even if it’s harmful to everyone involved.
content: This is the best insight in the essay, and it is a theorem. Boyd & Richerson (1992) showed that once punishment extends to those who fail to punish, it can stabilize cooperation in large groups — or, as their title says, “anything else,” including norms that harm everyone. Sociologists then showed the mechanism in people: individuals who privately reject a norm publicly enforce it, and sanction others for not enforcing it, to prove their own sincerity (Centola, Willer & Macy, 2005; experimentally, Willer, Kuwabara & Macy, 2009). The essay gets both the structure and the danger right.

quote: I wouldn’t be surprised to find it a human universal; it does have an obvious evolutionary rationale—one which would make it a very unpleasant and dangerous adaptation.
content: Asserted, not tested — and when tested, people turn out to be reluctant second-order punishers. In public-goods experiments that allowed it, participants were far more willing to reward those who rewarded cooperators than to punish those who failed to punish, and second-order punishment did little to sustain cooperation (Kiyonari & Barclay, 2008). The false-enforcement effect is real but is driven by fear of looking insincere, which is a social mechanism with a social remedy, not an adaptation. “Obvious evolutionary rationale” is the phrase the book warns about in Evolutionary Psychology.

quote: I certainly don’t believe in being “intolerant of intolerance,” as some inconsistently hold.
content: There is a well-known consistent version, and it is older than the essay's objection. Popper's paradox of tolerance (The Open Society and Its Enemies, 1945) argues that unlimited tolerance leads to the disappearance of tolerance, and so a tolerant society may withhold tolerance from those who would destroy it; Rawls (A Theory of Justice, §35) refines this to a rule of tolerating the intolerant unless they threaten the institutions of liberty. One can disagree with both. Calling the position “inconsistent” without meeting either formulation is a straw man.
